newsitem.title: UK: Forex market jittery ahead of G7.
newsitem.headline: Forex market jittery ahead of G7.

text.p: Foreign exchange traders are awaiting the G7 get-together in Washington with a little more trepidation than usual, amid fears that finance ministers will decide it time to prick the dollar's bubble.
The February Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Berlin sent a shiver through the market with its statement, "We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets...have been corrected."
But dollar bulls soon forgot any worries of concerted intervention and it has since risen another 4.0 percent on the mark and 3.5 percent on the yen.

"The problem with the Berlin G7 was that they didn't come out strongly against the rising dollar. There seemed no real objection from policy-makers (for strong dollar), so it was easy for the market to take the dollar higher," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.
"But the bias in the market has shifted. There is always a bit of nervousness into a G7 but this time the market is more likely to interpret the comments negatively to take the dollar lower."
Despite the raised tension this time, many in the market are still of the opinion that Japan is a lone voice in the wilderness calling for a reversal of the dollar's uptrend.
As with the Berlin meeting any hard-line comments from the U.S. and/or Germany will have a much bigger impact than more gripes from Japan.
"The risk is of a stronger comment by the U.S. or Germany," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
Germany has so far come up with unaggressive statements about the dollar's rise, saying only that mark's current level reflects fundamentals.
The U.S. also seems fairly relaxed despite the widening U.S. trade gap with Japan.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin last week said the U.S. dollar policy was unchanged, although his deputy Lawrence Summers said the U.S. would react strongly if trade pacts with Japan are violated.
"Summers is the bulldog on a leash and he's the one who has been barking," Coleman said. "Rubin is allowing Summers to do the dirty work in terms of the dollar's rise."
"If Rubin had been saying what Summers has been saying it would be a different story," he added.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto are due to meet on Friday and Japan must be keen to avert a potential flare-up in trade friction.
This is probably the main reason why Japan wants to see the dollar/yen come down.

Also, Japan must be worried about a sharp snap-back in dollar/yen when it finally does turn and with Japanese investor's massive exposure to overseas marekts the last thing Japan wants is a sharp dollar drop, analysts said.
So if the U.S. and Germany are relaxed about the dollar's rise, the ball is firmly in Japan's court and unilateral Bank of Japan intervention on dollar/yen is the main risk post-G7, analysts said.
But with the dollar yielding five percent more than the yen it is hard to see even aggressive central bank selling turning dollar/yen around, analysts said.
Japanese and U.S. officials agree that Japan should not continue to depend on an export led recovery and that Japan's economy is at last showing signs of improvement.
"This all backs up the idea of an eventual tightening of monetary policy but for now BoJ policy remains on hold and dollar/yen still looks bid," said Tony Norfield, Treasury Economist at ABN-Amro.
"Yet the main risk from the Washington G7 meeting is dollar/yen forex intervention."
